newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ample supply of cocoa keeps lid on physical market.
newsitem.headline: Ample supply of cocoa keeps lid on physical market.

text.p: Physical cocoa is being offered into the European market, keeping differentials under pressure but the chocolate industry remains a reluctant buyer and volumes traded are still low, European trade sources said on Friday.
"The sellers are a little long at the moment and the nearby differentials are low but industry is just sitting back and waiting," one trader said.

Traders said nearby Ivorian material was changing hands at 40 to 50 stg below March futures. In London, the benchmark March contract was down at just above 900 stg a tonne on Friday but turnover was light at just 961 lots during the morning session.
"This market is very puzzling. Everybody is talking about a market deficit this year, consumption is looking good but still the price drifts lower," one industry source said.
Traders said the ample availability of cocoa, and more importantly the perception of ample availability, was keeping prices under pressure, despite the forecasts of a deficit.

They said chocolate makers were content to take on only limited supplies of cocoa, replacing stocks as they used them and saw no need to hold large inventories. Their cover in general was estimated at between eight and nine months.

The physical trade in Europe has also been hampered by the growth in bulk shipments this year. The two major grinders in Amsterdam expect to bring in a significant percentage of their cocoa in bulk this year straight from origin.
"So much is straight coming into factories in bulk these days that the companies just don't need the physical market like they used to," said another trader.

Around 400,000 tonnes of cocoa is expected to be processed in the Netherlands in the 1996/97 season, up from 385,000 a year earlier with up to 250,000 tonnes arriving in bulk, more than double last year's total.
